title: private-deployments-reference-architectures-and-day2-ops-2026
author: Priya Shah
summary: Reference architectures, VPC deployment patterns, on‑prem packaging checklist, day‑2 operational runbooks, and upgrade & rollback procedures for Redwood Private deployments. This document is intended for Solutions Engineers, SRE, and customer platform teams preparing for VPC and on‑prem installations.
introduction: This page consolidates guidance for deploying Redwood Private in customer VPCs and on‑prem datacenters. It covers recommended reference architectures (single-tenant and multi-tenant), network and security requirements, packaging options (air-gapped and connected), day‑2 operations (monitoring, backups, scaling), and safe upgrade/rollback procedures including ownership and runbook links.
when_to_use_this_doc: Use this document during pre-sales scoping, implementation planning, and operational handover. If a customer requires HIPAA/PCI compliance, pair this doc with security-and-compliance/audit-logging and data-residency-and-retention pages.
architecture_overview: Redwood Private is deployed as two logical planes: Control Plane (Redwood-managed control services or customer-controlled private control plane) and Data Plane (customer VPC / on‑prem cluster that runs inference runtime). Common patterns: 1) VPC-hosted Private (recommended for cloud customers), 2) On‑prem air‑gapped bundle (recommended for regulated customers), 3) Hybrid (control plane in customer VPC + on‑prem GPUs). Each pattern includes separation of management, inference, and telemetry traffic to satisfy compliance and SLOs.
reference_architectures: We provide three validated reference architectures. High-level diagrams should be reviewed with customer networking teams prior to implementation. 1) VPC Single‑Tenant (dedicated subnets, NAT gateways, ILB for model endpoints). 2) VPC Multi‑Tenant (shared control plane, namespace isolation, per-customer quotas). 3) On‑Prem Air‑Gapped (OCI/VM template + physical rack network requirements). For each: list of deployable components, typical instance types, and recommended autoscaling bands.
network_and_security_requirements_table:
| Component | Port/Protocol | Source | Purpose |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Control Plane API | TCP 443 | Customer VPC egress or Private Peering | Management API and config sync |
| Telemetry (optional) | TCP 443 | Customer outbound to Redwood telemetry endpoints or internal ELK | Metrics/events |
| Inference ILB | TCP 80/443 | Application load balancer | Public/Private model endpoints |
| KV/Cache | TCP 11211 (or configured) | Internal subnets | KV-cache and prefix caching traffic |
| GPU Nodes | SSH TCP 22 | Admin CIDR | Debugging and runbook ops (restrict to bastion) |
| NFS/S3 access | TCP 443 / NFS ports | Internal or VPC endpoint | Model artifacts and checkpoints |

Notes: Use least privilege, curl tests during network validation, and enforce Security Groups with explicit CIDRs. for private-peering deploys, verify MTU >= 1500 and no transit proxies that break gRPC streams.
vpc_deployment_guide: Preconditions: customer provides VPC CIDRs, subnets for mgmt/inference/telemetry, DNS zone, and IAM role for S3 access. Steps: 1) Validate quotas (IP, ENIs, GPUs) with cloud provider. 2) Provision subnets: mgmt (private), inference (private with ILB), public bastion (optional). 3) Create VPC endpoints for S3/ECR/KMS where possible. 4) Configure Security Groups and NACLs per the network table. 5) Deploy control-plane connectors (Helm chart) to customer VPC or establish private peering to Redwood control plane. 6) Boot GPU node pool with preloaded container images (or use lazy-pull if bandwidth constrained). 7) Run post-deploy verification suite (listed below).
post_deploy_verification: 1) api-health: curl https://<control-plane>/health -> 200 OK and schema validation. 2) model-load: submit a canary request that loads model and returns valid tokens within latency SLO for canary (p50 < 120ms on 8xA10G baseline for text-gen small models). 3) telemetry-check: ensure metrics reach customer ELK or Redwood telemetry endpoint within 60s. 4) kv-cache-warm: verify prefix cache hit rate increases after repeated similar requests. 5) security-check: validate IAM roles and S3 access using read-only test artifact pull.
onprem_packaging_and_airgap: Packaging options: 1) Connected installer (Helm + operator, requires outbound to Redwood registries). 2) Air‑gapped bundle (tarball of Helm charts, OCI images as tar, and SHA256 sums). Air‑gapped checklist: 1) Confirm hardware inventory (GPU model, driver versions, NICs). 2) Validate OS image (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS recommended). 3) Provide internal registry and mirror images using provided mirroring scripts. 4) Verify KMS/HSM accessibility if customer requires external key management. 5) Run offline integrity checks (SHA256 sums) and load test images locally before scheduling migration windows.
day2_operations_runbook: Ownership: SRE (Redwood) owns platform-level playbooks; Customer platform team owns node lifecycle and local backups. Key runbooks: 1) Scaling: add GPU nodes via autoscaling group or K8s machine CR; drain and cordon nodes before termination. 2) Backups: model artifacts stored in S3-compatible store with lifecycle policy; backup PostgreSQL control-db nightly with point-in-time retention 7 days (configurable). 3) Incident triage: steps to gather logs, core dumps, and kernel traces. 4) Capacity alerts: setup alert when average GPU utilization > 75% for 15m or queue length > configured threshold. 5) Patching windows: schedule monthly security updates with canary node testing first.
upgrade_and_rollback_procedures: Principles: perform staged upgrades with canaries and automatic rollback on regressions. Pre-upgrade checklist: - Snapshot control-db - Freeze model promotions - Run test-suite on canary namespace - Verify runbook contact rotation. Upgrade steps: 1) Deploy control-plane upgrade to canary namespace (10% traffic). 2) Run synthetic traffic and perf/quality automated tests for 30m. 3) If metrics stable (no >5% latency regressions and no quality drop >1% on eval set), promote to 50% then 100%. 4) Upgrade data plane nodes using rolling update with maxUnavailable=1. Rollback steps: 1) Immediately switch traffic to previous control-plane version using traffic-mgr. 2) Stop in-flight deployments to data plane. 3) Restore DB snapshot if schema changes were applied and proved incompatible. 4) Open incident and follow postmortem playbook.
slo_and_safety_thresholds: Recommended SLOs and thresholds for customer deployments: - Control-plane API availability: 99.95% monthly. - Inference P95 latency (small text models): < 400ms under nominal load. - Model load success rate: > 99.5%. - Telemetry delivery: < 60s for metrics ingestion. Safety thresholds for automated rollback: any service error rate increase > 2x baseline sustained for 10m, or increase in failed model responses > 1% absolute.
observability_and_tools: Telemetry: Prometheus + Grafana primary on customer side; we ship Grafana dashboards and Prometheus scrape configs. Logs: Fluentd or Filebeat to central ELK/Opensearch. Tracing: optional Jaeger/OTLP collector. Recommended dashboards: per-model latency heatmap, request QPS and queue length, GPU utilization, KV cache hit-rate. Alerting: integrate with PagerDuty and email; use runbook links in alerts.
customer_requirements_library:
Minimum customer inputs required for scoping: 1) Expected QPS and concurrency profile. 2) Allowed latency SLOs and P95/P99 targets. 3) Compliance requirements (CCPA, HIPAA, PCI). 4) Network topology and connectivity options (private-peering, transit gateway, direct-connect). 5) Storage options (S3 endpoint, NFS, or local SSD), and retention windows. 6) Identity and secrets management (KMS provider, HSM access). 7) Maintenance window constraints and approved change windows. Use the following table during scoping:

| Field | Example | Required? |
|---|---|:--:|
| Target QPS | 2000 requests/min | Yes |
| Max P95 latency | 500ms | Yes |
| Peak concurrency | 100 | Yes |
| GPU type | NVIDIA A10G or A100 | Yes |
| Compliance | HIPAA | As needed |
| Outbound connectivity | Disabled (air-gapped) | Yes for air-gapped |
validation_and_acceptance_tests: Acceptance suite (run by SE + customer): 1) Functional: model inference correctness on golden prompts. 2) Load: sustained load for 60m at 1.5x expected QPS with no errors. 3) Failover: simulate node failure and ensure < 5% request drop and warmup within 120s. 4) Upgrade dry-run: perform canary upgrade and validate rollback mechanism. Document results and sign off with customer.
support_and_escalation: First responder: Customer platform engineer. Redwood support (Level 2) reachable via Support Slack #private-deployments and PagerDuty for severity P1. Escalation timeline: 15m initial ack, 1h mitigation plan, 4h cross-team engagement. Include incident template when filing: topology, versions, recent changes, logs, and synthetic test results.
appendix_and_artifacts:
Provided artifacts with every deployment: - Helm charts tarball with checksums - Air‑gap image bundle (if requested) - Terraform modules for VPC networking - Grafana dashboards JSON - Postgres schema migration scripts - Acceptance-test harness (k6 scripts)

Store artifact checksums in release manifest and include signed manifests in customer handover package.

faq:
Q: Is it possible to run control plane fully managed by Redwood? A: Yes, with private peering or VPN options; customers with strict compliance can request a private control plane deployed into their AWS account.
Q: What if GPU capacity is constrained? A: Use model quantization profiles and burst capacity options; consider Dedicated pools or hybrid on‑prem nodes.
Q: Who performs security audits? A: Security & compliance team partners with customer auditors; see security-and-compliance/compliance-evidence for evidence packages.
conclusion: This document is the canonical starting point for designing and operating Redwood Private deployments. For deployment-specific questions, contact Solutions Engineering. Maintain this page with upgrades to packaging, new reference architectures, and postmortem learnings.
